Electromagnetism

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 115k Articles: 1k
Electromagnetism describes how electric charge and electric current interact through the electric field E and magnetic field B. The Maxwell equations describe the fields and their sources; the Lorentz force describes the response of a particle of electric charge q and velocity v:
F=q(E+v×B),dtdEparticle​​=qE⋅v.
(1)
The electric field can change the particle's energy. The magnetic part of the Lorentz force is perpendicular to velocity, so magnetic forces do no work; they can bend a trajectory. These are local interactions: a particle responds to the electromagnetic field at its position. [ref].
The remarkable unification is that the same Maxwell equations connect Coulomb's law, Faraday's law of induction, and freely propagating electromagnetic waves. A changing electric field contributes to magnetic circulation through displacement current; together with Faraday's law, this permits waves in vacuum without conducting matter. The Poynting theorem then explains how the fields store and transport energy. This connects the force on a charge to the energy carried by light.
In his 1865 paper, James Clerk Maxwell derived transverse disturbances and compared the propagation speed inferred from electrical measurements with independently measured light speeds. Part VI, especially §§95–97, argues that their agreement supports identifying light as an electromagnetic wave. This was a comparison with finite experimental accuracy, rather than a numerical identity between the historical measurements. [ref]; [ref].

Quasistatic electromagnetic approximation

Words: 85
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
A quasistatic electromagnetic approximation neglects propagation delay over a vacuum device of characteristic size L when ωL/c≪1. It does not automatically discard every time derivative: an Ampere-Maxwell law calculation in a capacitor gap must retain displacement current. In a medium use the relevant propagation and response scales. The dominant approximately static electric field can be used to calculate a smaller induced magnetic field, provided the corrections to the dominant field remain small. Near a resonance or for a large distributed circuit, the size criterion alone may not justify an instantaneous lumped model.

Dielectrophoresis

Words: 50 Articles: 1
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
Motion driven by the force on induced polarization in a nonuniform electric field. In the dipole regime its sign depends on the particle–medium polarizability contrast and its magnitude scales with particle volume.

Clausius-Mossotti factor (K(ω))

Words: 18
Dielectrophoresis OurBigBook.com
The spherical-particle polarization-contrast factor K=(ϵp​−ϵm​)/(ϵp​+2ϵm​). Its real part controls ordinary time-averaged dielectrophoresis in the quasistatic dipole approximation.

Reciprocity (electromagnetism)

Words: 43
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
Electromagnetic reciprocity relates the response obtained after exchanging source and receiver in a linear reciprocal medium. For suitably normalized ports it gives a symmetric scattering matrix. It does not require zero reflection. A magnetically biased Faraday effect provides an important optical example in which reciprocity can fail.

Electricity concerns phenomena associated with electric charge, including electric fields and electric currents.

Electromagnetic induction

Words: 418 Articles: 10
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
Electromagnetic induction includes an induced electromotive force associated with a changing magnetic field or motion of a conductor in a magnetic field. Faraday's law of induction and motional electromotive force specify the relevant contributions.

Homopolar generator (E=ωBa2/2)

Words: 44
Electromagnetic induction OurBigBook.com
For a conducting disc of radius a rotating in a uniform axial magnetic field B, the shaft-to-rim motional electromotive force is ∫0a​ωrBdr=ωBa2/2. A current I between shaft and rim gives the opposing torque IBa2/2, making electromagnetic conversion power EI equal to mechanical torque times angular speed.

Magnetic braking

Words: 283 Articles: 6
Electromagnetic induction OurBigBook.com
Braking caused by induced currents whose magnetic force opposes motion. energy removed from mechanical motion can become resistive heat; the force depends on magnetic-field gradients or boundary crossing, resistance and inductance.

Resistive magnetic entry of a falling loop (τ=mR/(Ba)2)

Words: 61
Magnetic braking OurBigBook.com
A rectangular loop entering a uniform magnetic field while only one horizontal segment is immersed has motional electromotive force Bav. Neglecting self-inductance, its electric current is Bav/R and its upward magnetic force is (Ba)2v/R. The equation mv˙=mg−(Ba)2v/R gives exponential relaxation toward mgR/(Ba)2. This entry model ends when both horizontal segments enter the field; then their net magnetic force and the rate of change of external magnetic flux vanish.

Rotational magnetic damping of a square wire loop

Words: 45
Magnetic braking OurBigBook.com
A thin square loop rotating about a central in-plane axis has I=ma2/6. With ohmic current and decay slow compared with a rotation, the averaged torque is −B2a4ω/(2R). Its angular-speed decay time is mR/(3B2a2); its kinetic-energy decay time is half that value.

Translational magnetic damping of a square wire loop

Words: 35
Magnetic braking OurBigBook.com
A square wire loop partly in a uniform field has linear drag B2a2v/R, giving velocity-relaxation time τt​=mR/(B2a2). For uniform wire of mass density ρm​ and resistivity ρe​, τt​=16ρm​ρe​/B2, independent of wire dimensions.

Electrical and mechanical time scales in magnetic braking

Words: 29
Magnetic braking OurBigBook.com
The instantaneous-current approximation uses I=E/R and requires the electrical relaxation time L/R to be negligible relative to the relevant mechanical changes. Otherwise circuit self-inductance changes the braking transient.

Loop crossing a magnetic field boundary

Words: 85 Articles: 1
Magnetic braking OurBigBook.com
A square resistive loop of side a, moving normally across a sharp field edge at speed v, has induced current magnitude Bav/R and drag magnitude B2a2v/R while partially overlapping the field. Completely enclosed in a uniform static field it has no changing flux and, with neglected self-inductance, no current.
Impulse of magnetic braking
Words: 35
Loop crossing a magnetic field boundary OurBigBook.com
For a complete entry and exit of a small square loop, integrating the drag over two distances a gives impulse magnitude 2B2a3/R. This is independent of speed in the ideal sharp-edge, zero-inductance model, though dissipated energy is not.

Inductive impulse outside a switched solenoid

Words: 54
Electromagnetic induction OurBigBook.com
Changing the magnetic flux through a long solenoid produces an exterior azimuthal electric field Eϕ​(r,t)=−Φ˙(t)/(2πr) by Faraday's law of induction. A charge q whose displacement is negligible during the switching receives mechanical momentum
Δp=−2πrqΔΦ​ϕ^​.
(2)
The result assumes the usual quasistatic field approximation and neglects the particle's displacement while the pulse acts. It describes an electromagnetic induction effect, distinct from the static Aharonov-Bohm effect.

Lorenz-gauge reduction of the electromagnetic action

Words: 64
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
The electromagnetic field tensor action differs from the component-gradient potential action by (2μ0​)−1∫∂bAa∂a​Ab​d4x. Integration by parts expresses this term as a boundary integral plus (2μ0​)−1∫(∂a​Aa)2d4x. With the Lorenz gauge and fixed or vanishing boundary data, the two actions therefore differ only by a boundary term. Varying the component-gradient action without restriction gives the potential wave equations; the Lorenz condition must be supplied to recover all Maxwell equations.

Volume conductor

Words: 273 Articles: 4
Bioelectromagnetism OurBigBook.com
A volume conductor is a conducting three-dimensional medium through which electric currents flow. In the quasistatic bioelectric model, the total current density is J=Jp−σ∇u, comprising an impressed source current and its Ohmic return current. Electric charge conservation gives ∇⋅(σ∇u)=∇⋅Jp. An insulating boundary has zero normal total current.

Geselowitz formula (B=Bp−4πμ0​σ​∫S​un′×∣r−r′∣3r−r′​dS′)

Words: 60
Volume conductor OurBigBook.com
For a homogeneous volume conductor with an insulating boundary S, the Geselowitz formula expresses the exterior magnetic field as the primary Biot-Savart law field minus a surface contribution from the induced electric potential. For a current dipole, Bp=μ0​Q×(r−r0​)/(4π∣r−r0​∣3). On a spherical boundary, n′ is parallel to r′, so the surface term has zero radial component at the observation point.

Spherical volume conductor model (∣r∣<a)

Words: 168 Articles: 2
Volume conductor OurBigBook.com
A spherical volume conductor model approximates a conducting body by a sphere, usually with uniform or radially stratified conductivity. It provides explicit forward models for electroencephalography and magnetoencephalography. Its symmetry makes a radial current dipole magnetically silent outside the sphere; departures from spherical symmetry need not retain that property.
Sarvas formula (B=4πμ0​​∇F(Q×r0​)⋅r​)
Words: 127 Articles: 1
Spherical volume conductor model OurBigBook.com
For the exterior of a spherical volume conductor model, put P=∣r−r0​∣, r=∣r∣ and F=rP2+Pr⋅(r−r0​). The displayed Sarvas formula follows by taking the radial component of the Geselowitz formula and integrating the magnetic scalar potential from infinity. It is independent of a spherically symmetric conductivity profile. The sign shown uses B=+μ0​∇U/(4π); conventions defining a magnetic potential with a minus sign reverse U. Sarvas's original paper derives the spherical-conductor field and its consequences for the inverse problem.
Spherical current-dipole logarithmic kernel (ϕ=b1​logr+P−br+P+b​,b=∣r0​∣)
Words: 50
Sarvas formula OurBigBook.com
For r>b and P=∣r−r0​∣, the displayed kernel satisfies ϕ=∫r∞​ds/[s∣sr−r0​∣]. The limit at b=0 is 1/r. Differentiating along Q×r0​, which preserves b, gives (Q×r0​)⋅∇r0​​ϕ=(Q×r0​)⋅r/F. Thus it generates the normalized magnetic scalar potential in the Sarvas formula.

Maxwell–Chern–Simons one-form equation (d∗F+kF=0)

Words: 64
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
For a differential one-form A on an oriented three-dimensional spacetime, varying 21​∫(F∧∗F+kA∧F), with F=dA, gives d∗F+kF=0. With signature (−,+,+), ∗2=−1 on one- and two-forms; writing B=∗F gives dB−k∗B=0 and the identity d∗B=0. An Abelian gauge transformation changes the action by 2k​∫∂M​ΛF. Thus the bulk field equation is invariant, while invariance of the integrated action depends on boundary conditions.

Capacitor

Words: 3k Articles: 18
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
A capacitor stores electrostatic energy by separating electric charge between two electrical conductors. In the ideal two-terminal model their electric charges are +Q and −Q, with a vacuum or insulating gap preventing direct transfer between them. Write V=ϕ+​−ϕ−​ for the terminal electric potential difference, where ϕ+​ and ϕ−​ are the electric potentials of the two electrical conductors. A linear capacitor obeys
Q=CV,
(3)
where its capacitance C depends on the geometry and permittivity, and is independent of the applied electric potential difference while these stay fixed. [ref].
For example, the parallel-plate capacitor below has capacitance C=88.54pF. At terminal electric potential difference V=10V, the electric charge magnitude on either plate is
Q=CV=(8.854×10−11)(10)C=8.854×10−10C=0.8854nC.
(4)
The total electric charge of the device is Q+(−Q)=0: charge neutrality does not imply zero capacitor energy. This capacitor stores 4.427nJ in its electric field. The schematic in parallel-plate capacitor shows the separation of electric charge; the plots in capacitor energy show how storage grows with terminal electric potential difference.
The useful distinction is between storing net electric charge and storing separated electric charge. A capacitor can release electrostatic energy into an electrical circuit; in an ideal RLC circuit, energy moves between the capacitor's electric field and the magnetic field associated with inductance. An ideal disconnected capacitor retains its separated electric charges and capacitor energy because there is no path for discharge.

Parallel-plate capacitor (C=ϵA/d)

Words: 2k Articles: 7
Capacitor OurBigBook.com
A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two parallel electrical conductors with overlapping area A and separation d. If the gap is small compared with both plate widths and is filled by a uniform material of positive permittivity ϵ, its capacitance is approximately
C≃dϵA​.
(5)
This neglects the fringing field of a capacitor near the plate edges. The interior electric field points from the plate of positive electric charge to the plate of negative electric charge, and is approximately uniform. [ref].
For a worked vacuum example, stipulate A=0.01m2, d=0.001m, and vacuum permittivity ϵ0​≈8.854×10−12F/m. This rounds the value in Fundamental Physical Constants — Complete Listing by National Institute of Standards and Technology and others. Within the approximation,
C≃0.001(8.854×10−12)(0.01)​F=8.854×10−11F=88.54pF.
(6)
At terminal electric potential difference V=10V, the electric field magnitude is E≃V/d=104V/m, the plate electric charge magnitude is Q=CV=0.8854nC, and the capacitor energy is U=CV2/2=4.427nJ. These numbers use the stipulated rounded vacuum permittivity; finite plates also have corrections from the fringing field of a capacitor.
The formula makes design changes easy to predict: doubling the overlapping area doubles the capacitance, and halving the gap doubles the capacitance, with permittivity fixed and the fringing field of a capacitor neglected. Doubling permittivity also doubles capacitance if the material uniformly fills the gap and remains linear. This lets a compact device store more separated electric charge at the same terminal electric potential difference.
The short derivation uses surface charge density σ=Q/A. In the interior, Gauss's law gives electric field magnitude E≃σ/ϵ=Q/(ϵA). The electric potential difference is V≃Ed=Qd/(ϵA), so dividing Q by V gives C≃ϵA/d. A narrow curved capacitor gap has the same leading local approximation when its width is much less than the curvature radius.

Fringing field of a capacitor

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Parallel-plate capacitor OurBigBook.com
The fringing field of a capacitor is the nonuniform electric field near the edges of its electrical conductors, extending outside the gap. For a parallel-plate capacitor, neglecting it is useful when the gap is much smaller than both plate widths; the approximation C≃ϵA/d is less reliable when these lengths become comparable.
Finite plates break the translational symmetry of the infinite-plate model. Each conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential, so the electric field must meet a smooth conducting surface normally. Near an edge, the equipotentials curve into the surrounding space and the electric field changes both direction and magnitude. The surface charge density adjusts to enforce the conducting boundary conditions; it is not uniform all the way to a sharp edge. The electrostatic boundary conditions at a conductor explain why zero electric field inside the metal does not imply zero electric field just outside it.
The practical issue is where the nearly uniform region ends. A probe near the centre can support E≃V/d while a probe close to an edge detects a lateral component and a different magnitude. A total capacitance reading also includes electric flux outside the simple footprint. The fringing field of a capacitor can therefore matter in permittivity measurements even when a central electric field measurement looks nearly ideal. Keysight's three-electrode fixture diverts the fringe contribution away from the measured response.[ref]

Capacitor gap aspect ratio (η=d/W)
Words: 322
Fringing field of a capacitor OurBigBook.com
The capacitor gap aspect ratio compares the gap d with a lateral plate width W. For rectangular plates of widths Wx​,Wz​, require both d/Wx​≪1 and d/Wz​≪1 for the leading parallel-plate capacitor approximation. Large area alone is insufficient: a long narrow strip can have large area and still have d comparable with its smaller width. In addition, the observation point must be many gap widths from an edge. Reducing d/W improves the interior approximation without making the edge itself disappear.
In a two-dimensional straight gap, write the electric potential as the infinite-plate solution plus a perturbation:
ϕ(x,y)=dV​y+δϕ(x,y),−2d​<y<2d​.
(7)
The perturbation satisfies the Laplace equation and vanishes on the two ideal plates. Separation of variables in a semi-infinite strip, with s the distance inward from its entrance, gives transverse modes
δϕn​(s,y)=an​e−nπs/dsin(dnπ(y+d/2)​),n=1,2,….
(8)
Thus edge disturbances have a natural penetration scale set by d. Modes forbidden by a particular symmetry have zero coefficients; this expression is an explanation of localization in an ideal strip, not a universal numerical correction to finite-plate capacitance. The outside boundary conditions determine the coefficients.
There is no single aspect-ratio cutoff guaranteeing an assigned accuracy: the requested observable, plate shape and thickness, surroundings, dielectric distribution, and guard geometry all matter. The small-gap approximation is local and is not uniform across an edge. It also does not justify extrapolating C≃ϵA/d to arbitrarily large d, where finite electrical conductors and their external electric field dominate. At fixed V, formally shrinking an ideal gap makes the interior electric field grow like 1/d; real electric currents across an imperfectly insulating gap, surface roughness and contact eventually invalidate that ideal limit.
Bounded two-dimensional capacitor field model (∂x2​ϕ+∂y2​ϕ=0)
Words: 335
Fringing field of a capacitor OurBigBook.com
The diagrams solve an explicitly bounded Dirichlet problem in a uniform charge-free medium of constant permittivity. Take a width scale W=1 and terminal electric potential difference V=1. Two zero-thickness ideal plate segments occupy ∣x∣≤W/2 at y=±d/2, with electric potentials ±V/2. Fix ϕ=0 on the entire rectangle x=±2W, y=±1.5W. This boundary is an additional enclosing equipotential, rather than a condition at infinity. The model is invariant along the omitted third direction. The connection between the electric potential, its gradient, and the charge-free Laplace equation follows from electrostatics.[ref]
On a square mesh of spacing h=W/160, the finite difference method imposes
ϕi,j​=41​(ϕi+1,j​+ϕi−1,j​+ϕi,j+1​+ϕi,j−1​)
(9)
at free nodes, while plate and outer nodes retain their prescribed electric potentials. There are 641×481 nodes. Each plotted gap aligns exactly with the mesh; the smallest gap has 16 mesh intervals. The generators solve the resulting linear system by the Conjugate gradient method, stopping when the maximum dimensionless five-point residual is below 2×10−10, and use central finite differences to approximate E=−∇ϕ away from plate nodes.
The discrete maximum principle keeps the computed electric potential between −V/2 and +V/2. Reflection checks require evenness in x and oddness in y; halving h tests discretization effects, while enlarging the outer rectangle tests sensitivity to its artificial boundary conditions. These are different checks: a small residual only establishes that the discrete equations were solved. Differentiating near zero-thickness endpoints is especially sensitive to the mesh, so the plots do not report a converged edge peak. No total electric charge, exact open-domain three-dimensional capacitance, or measured material property is extracted from this model.
For a bounded numerical check, compare h=W/80 with the plotted h=W/160 at midplane positions x/W=0,0.25,0.40,0.50,0.60,0.80. At d/W=0.10, the largest change in −Ey​d/V is approximately 0.0265, at x/W=0.50; the other five sampled changes are below 0.00472. At d/W=0.25, moving the outer rectangle from ±2W×±1.5W to ±3W×±2W while retaining h=W/80 changes these samples by at most approximately 0.00622. These calculated sensitivities support the qualitative comparison and expose its limits; they are not experimental uncertainties or evidence that the artificial boundary has converged to infinity.
Mapping a capacitor fringing field
Words: 415
Fringing field of a capacitor OurBigBook.com
The Field Mapper Kit (PK-9023), Product Manual 012-04346D by PASCO scientific (p. 3, Parallel plate capacitor) proposes a direct investigation of the plate-length-to-gap ratio using conductive-paper electric potential mapping. Its finite straight electrodes represent a cross-section of the plates. The apparatus is a gridded resistive sheet on a corkboard, silver-ink electrodes, pushpin electrical contacts, a 5–20V direct supply capable of 25mA, and a voltmeter with input electrical resistance at least 10MΩ. The manual specifies waiting 20 minutes for the ink to reach its maximum electrical conductivity, then checking each electrode: its internal voltage drop should be no more than 1% of the applied electric potential difference.[ref]
For the readout, keep one voltmeter lead on the reference electrode and scan the other across the sheet. Mark points having the same reading to trace an equipotential. A second method holds the two probe tips at a fixed separation and pivots them to find the largest electric potential difference; a suggested separation is one centimetre. Avoid printed grid marks when making contact.[ref]
The inference follows from the measured electric potential, rather than assuming straight electric field lines. With probe separation Δs and direction t, a local finite difference gives
E⋅t≃−Δsϕ(P+Δst)−ϕ(P)​.
(10)
An arrow toward rising electric potential follows +∇ϕ, so it must be reversed to show E. To investigate the fringing field of a capacitor, compare contours well inside the gap with contours near and beyond the ends, then repeat at a changed gap while keeping the sheet boundary and plate length fixed. Curving contours and an outside gradient establish nonuniformity in this planar setup. Compare −Ey​d/V at recorded positions to distinguish simple voltage rescaling from geometric changes; no measured values are supplied here.
Additional useful controls are repeat reference readings to detect drift, reversal of supply polarity, and repeating selected readings with reduced probe spacing. Keep contact quality and sheet edges fixed during the aspect-ratio comparison. Finite probe separation averages the gradient; reducing it improves spatial resolution but magnifies the effect of voltage uncertainty. Voltmeter loading, imperfect ink electrodes, and inhomogeneous sheet electrical conductivity can mimic distortions. These proposed checks supplement the manufacturer's electrode check, rather than claiming a completed experiment.
The sheet carries a steady electric current. For uniform electrical conductivity, Ohm's law and electric charge conservation give the two-dimensional Laplace equation away from electrodes, as explained in conductive-paper electric potential mapping. Uncontacted sheet edges have zero normal electric current, whereas the diagram model fixes zero outer electric potential. These distinct boundary conditions must be matched before a quantitative comparison. The apparatus reveals a planar electric potential map; it does not directly measure the free-space three-dimensional capacitance of metal plates.
Guard electrode of a capacitor
Words: 159
Fringing field of a capacitor OurBigBook.com
A guard electrode of a capacitor surrounds an electrically isolated sensing electrode and is held at the same electric potential. The small insulating slot separates their readout paths. The guard extends the nearly planar equipotential, moving the main outer edge away from the sensing region; it does not abolish the fringing field of a capacitor everywhere. In a capacitance fixture, fringe electric current is routed through the guard instead of the sensing readout. Keysight describes this three-electrode method in Materials Measurement: Dielectric Materials (Solution, 16451B fixture).[ref]
Measuring the sensing and guard electric currents together would include the diverted response again. Grounding an arbitrary surrounding electrode also does not reproduce a guard unless its electric potential matches the sensing electrode. Finite guard width, the insulating slot, plate misalignment and specimen air gaps limit the approximation. Use capacitance measurement calibration and the geometry appropriate to the sensing region when inferring permittivity. The source also warns that guarding changes the electromagnetic field unfavourably at high frequency, so the low-frequency electrostatic picture has a restricted range.[ref]

Capacitor energy (U=Q2/(2C))

Words: 554 Articles: 3
Capacitor OurBigBook.com
The capacitor energy is the electrostatic energy stored when electric charge is separated. For a linear capacitor of fixed positive capacitance C, plate electric charge magnitude Q, and terminal electric potential difference V=Q/C, it is
U=2CQ2​=21​CV2=21​QV.
(11)
The zero is the uncharged state. Thus the capacitor energy is positive for nonzero Q, even though the total electric charge of the two plates is zero. [ref].
For the parallel-plate capacitor example, capacitance C=8.854×10−11F and terminal electric potential difference V=10V give
U=21​(8.854×10−11)(10)2J=4.427×10−9J=4.427nJ.
(12)
The plate electric charge magnitude is Q=0.8854nC. Doubling terminal electric potential difference with capacitance unchanged doubles the plate electric charge magnitude and quadruples the capacitor energy.
The electric charge is a linear function of terminal electric potential difference, while capacitor energy is a quadratic function. The second curve in each plot uses twice the capacitance: at a given terminal electric potential difference, both plate electric charge magnitude and capacitor energy double. These relations let us calculate how much energy an electrical circuit can receive when a capacitor discharges.
A brief charging argument explains the factor 1/2. If the plate electric charge magnitude has reached q, the terminal electric potential difference is q/C. Transferring a further amount dq of electric charge quasistatically requires work dW=(q/C)dq. With the geometry and permittivity fixed, the integral is
U=∫0Q​Cq​dq=2CQ2​.
(13)
Using Q=CV gives the other two forms. This integral accounts for the gradually rising terminal electric potential difference; it is the work stored in the capacitor's electric field, rather than a claim that all energy drawn from a fixed-voltage battery during charging ends up stored.
The field picture gives the same result. In the vacuum gap of a parallel-plate capacitor, the electric field has energy density u=ϵ0​E2/2. Multiplying by the gap volume Ad gives the electrostatic energy
U≃21​ϵ0​E2Ad=21​dϵ0​A​V2=21​CV2.
(14)
For the worked example, u=4.427×10−4J/m3 and Ad=10−5m3 reproduce U=4.427nJ. The electrostatic energy resides in the electric field throughout the gap, despite overall charge neutrality.
When capacitance changes, specify the constraint. At fixed plate electric charge magnitude Q, increasing capacitance decreases capacitor energy Q2/(2C); doubling capacitance halves it. At fixed terminal electric potential difference V, increasing capacitance increases capacitor energy CV2/2; doubling capacitance doubles it. In the latter case a connected battery supplies additional electric charge and energy, and there may also be mechanical work. Use the fixed-voltage capacitor energy balance to account for all transfers before inferring a force from changing capacitor energy.

Fixed-voltage capacitor energy balance (dUfield​=dWmech​+VdQ)

Words: 164 Articles: 1
Capacitor energy OurBigBook.com
For a quasistatic change of capacitance at fixed terminal electric potential difference, the capacitor energy is U=CV2/2 and plate electric charge is Q=CV. Electrical work supplied to the electric field by the battery is VdQ, so mechanical work done on the capacitor is dWmech​=dU−VdQ=−V2dC/2. Increasing the separation of a parallel-plate capacitor makes dC<0: mechanical work is positive even though electrostatic energy decreases, because electrical energy returns to the source. Conversely, when dC>0, the battery supplies V2dC: half increases capacitor energy and half is available as mechanical work done by the electric field. Differentiating capacitor energy alone at fixed terminal electric potential difference omits this exchange with the battery.

Capacitance (C)

Words: 885 Articles: 12
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
The capacitance of a linear two-terminal capacitor is the constant relating its separated electric charge to its terminal electric potential difference:
Q=CV,C=VQ​(V=0).
(15)
Here Q is the electric charge on one electrical conductor, the other carries −Q, and V is their electric potential difference with the same ordering. Reversing the terminal ordering reverses both Q and V and leaves capacitance unchanged. An ideal passive capacitor has C≥0; an ordinary pair of separated electrical conductors with positive permittivity has C>0. At V=0, use Q=CV rather than the undefined ratio 0/0.
For example, electric charge magnitude Q=0.8854nC at terminal electric potential difference V=10V gives capacitance C=88.54pF. At 20V, the same linear capacitor has Q=1.7708nC and the same capacitance. The plots in capacitor energy show that capacitance is the slope of the electric charge versus terminal electric potential difference graph.
For fixed geometry and linear material response, capacitance depends on dimensions and permittivity, rather than the source's terminal electric potential difference. This is why capacitance is a useful property of a component: once it is known, Q=CV predicts the separated electric charge for each operating terminal electric potential difference. The SI unit is the farad, 1F=1C/V. [ref].
For combinations of capacitors, the same terminal definition gives an equivalent capacitance. Two identical capacitors of capacitance C connected in parallel share the same terminal electric potential difference, and their electric charges add, giving Ceq​=2C. Connected in series with an initially neutral isolated junction, they carry equal plate electric charge magnitudes and their terminal electric potential differences add, giving Ceq​=C/2. [ref].

Two isolated conducting drops of radius a and equal charge merge at fixed total charge and volume. The new radius is 21/3a, so its capacitance grows by only 21/3 while total charge doubles. Relative to the sum of the initially separated self energies, the final electric field energy grows by 22/3. Decreased surface energy and/or applied mechanical work can supply that increase. Sufficiently large like charges need not coalesce spontaneously; energy conservation is not a guarantee of merging. A maintained external voltage would define a different problem.

For a parallel-plate capacitor of area A and separation d, filled by a spatially varying positive scalar permittivity, neglect edge fields. Inductance (L)

Words: 1k Articles: 15
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
Inductance relates electric currents to the magnetic flux linkage they produce. For a single linear coil with fixed geometry and magnetic response, its self-inductance L is the constant in
Λ=LI.
(20)
Here Λ is magnetic flux linkage from the coil's own electric current I. The SI unit of inductance is the henry. Knowing inductance lets us predict the induced electromotive force when electric current changes, and the magnetic energy stored by an inductor. [ref].
For example, a coil of self-inductance 0.5H carrying electric current 3A has magnetic flux linkage 1.5Wb. If its 100 turns link the same magnetic flux, each turn has magnetic flux 0.015Wb. Keeping the geometry and magnetic response fixed while doubling electric current doubles magnetic flux linkage and quadruples the inductor's magnetic energy.
The comparison with capacitance is useful: a linear capacitor has Q=CV and stores capacitor energy CV2/2 in its electric field, whereas a linear inductor has Λ=LI and stores magnetic energy LI2/2 in its magnetic field. The RLC circuit brings both forms of energy storage together.

Inductance OurBigBook.com
Self-inductance is inductance associated with a coil's own electric current, rather than magnetic flux supplied by another coil. In the linear model, fixed geometry and magnetic response give constant L in Λ=LI. With the turn orientations defined in magnetic flux linkage, Faraday's law of induction gives the self-induced electromotive force
Eind​=−dtdΛ​=−LdtdI​.
(23)
The final equality requires constant L; if the geometry changes, use −dΛ/dt. The minus sign expresses Lenz's law: the induced electromotive force opposes the change in electric current. It does not always oppose the electric current itself. When positive electric current decreases, the induced electromotive force acts in its direction. [ref].
For terminal sign bookkeeping, label the ideal inductor's terminals a,b, choose positive electric current entering a and leaving b, and define vL​ as the terminal electric potential difference drop from a to b in the lumped electrical circuit model. This passive convention gives
vL​=+LdtdI​=−Eind​.
(24)
Thus a coil with self-inductance 0.5H and increasing electric current dI/dt=12A/s has terminal drop vL​=6V and induced electromotive force Eind​=−6V. These signs describe the same process with different reference conventions. The RL circuit uses the terminal-drop convention throughout.
A finite terminal electric potential difference cannot make the electric current of an ideal inductor with constant L>0 jump. Integrating its differential equation gives
I(t2​)−I(t1​)=L1​∫t1​t2​​vL​(t)dt.
(25)
If vL​ stays bounded, the integral tends to zero as the interval shrinks, ensuring continuity of electric current. A step in terminal electric potential difference changes dI/dt immediately, while electric current remains continuous. At constant electric current, the self-induced electromotive force is zero, although the inductor's magnetic energy can remain nonzero.

An inductor is an electrical circuit component designed to provide self-inductance, often a coil such as a solenoid. An ideal linear inductor has constant L>0 and zero electrical resistance. Its stored magnetic energy, with zero chosen at zero electric current, is
U=21​LI2.
(26)
For self-inductance 0.5H and electric current 3A, this gives U=2.25J. Unlike Joule heating, ideal storage is recoverable: the inductor can return energy to an electrical circuit when its electric current decreases. [ref].
The short derivation uses the terminal convention in self-inductance. The power absorbed by an ideal inductor is
PL​=vL​I=LIdtdI​=dtd​(21​LI2).
(27)
Starting from zero electric current, the integral of this power gives
U=∫0t​PL​(t′)dt′=∫0I​Lidi=21​LI2.
(28)
Positive PL​ increases stored magnetic energy; negative PL​ returns energy. At constant electric current 3A in the example, PL​=0 and induced electromotive force is zero, but U=2.25J still resides in the magnetic field. The battery in the steady RL circuit supplies Joule heating in the electrical resistance, rather than further increasing the inductor's magnetic energy.
During the closed-loop release in RL circuit, stored magnetic energy plus accumulated Joule heating stays 2.25J. A real coil also has electrical resistance, so its Joule heating must be included separately from ideal inductor storage. The constant-L formulas assume a fixed linear magnetic response.

Magnetization is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume, described by a vector field M(r). Average the microscopic magnetic dipole moments in a small region of volume ΔV around the point r:
M(r)≃ΔV1​∑i∈ΔV​mi​,mtotal​=∫V​MdV.
(31)
The averaging region should contain many microscopic constituents while being small compared with the distance over which the macroscopic magnetization varies. With number density n of identical constituents, this becomes M=n⟨m⟩. Magnetic dipole moment has SI units Am2, so magnetization has units A/m: amperes per metre. The average is a vector sum, not a sum of magnitudes.[ref]
Alignment can change magnetization without changing the magnitude of any individual magnetic dipole moment. In a constructed counting example, eight equal magnetic dipole moments of magnitude m0​ occupy the same volume ΔV. Six along +z and two along −z give M=4m0​z/ΔV; turning the two opposing magnetic dipole moments to +z doubles magnetization to 8m0​z/ΔV. Both arrangements have the same sum of magnitudes, 8m0​. Changing the individual magnetic dipole moments provides another possible response; their alignment and their magnitudes are distinct ingredients. Microscopic spin contributes magnetic dipole moment without being a literal rotating charged ball.
Distinguish magnetization M, magnetic field B, and magnetic field intensity H. In SI,
B=μ0​(H+M),[M]=[H]=A/m,[B]=T.
(32)
Here μ0​ is the vacuum permeability, and T denotes the tesla. Magnetization describes matter's magnetic dipole moment density; magnetic field enters the Lorentz force; magnetic field intensity separates the free electric current contribution in the macroscopic equations. In particular, zero applied magnetic field does not generally imply H=0 inside a finite magnet: its demagnetizing field depends on shape.[ref]
For stationary electric polarization, magnetization produces bound current in the volume and on its bounding surface:
Jb​=∇×M,Kb​=M×n.
(33)
The curl gives a current density in A/m2; Kb​ is a surface current density in A/m. The unit normal n points outward from the magnetized material into a region with zero magnetization. Across an interface between two magnetized media, the net bound current sheet is
Kinterface​=(M1​−M2​)×n,
(34)
where the unit normal points from medium 1 to medium 2. Both faces contribute: medium 2 has the opposite outward normal vector. This fixes the cross product sign. If electric polarization changes with time, add its contribution ∂t​P to the bound current.[ref]
A short proof outline explains why both contributions are needed. Write Mext​=MχV​, where χV​ is the indicator function of the material's volume. In the sense of distributions, its gradient is ∇χV​=−nδS​, with δS​ the surface delta distribution. The product rule for the curl gives
∇×(χV​M)=χV​∇×M+(M×n)δS​.
(35)
Thus a constant interior magnetization can have zero interior curl and still produce a nonzero boundary electric current. Equivalently, neighboring ideal microscopic current loops cancel along shared edges while uncompensated edges remain on the outside. This bound current representation predicts the same macroscopic magnetic field as the magnetization distribution; it does not require a wire or free charge transport around the magnet. Its usefulness is that the familiar Biot-Savart law can now calculate the magnetic field from a specified magnetization.
A time-dependent average magnetization need not vary smoothly under a smooth drive. The Barkhausen effect resolves collective jumps through their induced electromotive force; Barkhausen pulse area explains how that derivative readout relates to the underlying change.

Vibrating-sample magnetometer

Words: 274
Magnetization OurBigBook.com
A vibrating-sample magnetometer measures a specimen's magnetic dipole moment through the induced electromotive force as it moves relative to stationary pickup coils. Dividing that magnetic dipole moment by the specimen's independently determined volume gives its average magnetization.
In Simon Foner's 1959 apparatus, the specimen was weighed and glued to a mount. A loudspeaker drive moved it perpendicular to an applied uniform magnetic field between magnet poles; stationary coils detected the induced electromotive force. A reference magnet on the same vibrating assembly generated a second coil electromotive force. Adjusting the reference voltage divider to an electrical null compared the specimen signal with this reference. The measurement calibration substituted a magnetically saturated pure nickel sphere of known magnetic dipole moment; a specimen-removed reading corrected the mount's contribution. The calibrated signal inferred the specimen's magnetic dipole moment, not its local magnetization map. Measurement uncertainty in the standard, positioning, finite specimen size, coil noise, and mechanical coupling limited the inference.[ref]
The readout follows Faraday's law of induction. In a small-displacement model with constant projected magnetic dipole moment m, let the pickup-coil magnetic flux linkage be Φ(z)=g(z)m and the specimen motion be z(t)=z0​+acosωt. Here g incorporates coil geometry and turn count, a is the displacement amplitude, and ω is angular frequency. To first order in displacement, with g′(z0​) the derivative at the mean position,
V(t)=−dtdΦ​≃mg′(z0​)aωsinωt.
(40)
This is an original idealized readout relation: a larger induced electromotive force can mean larger magnetic dipole moment, greater motion, or a changed coil position. A synchronously moving reference allows common motion factors to cancel in the ratio of induced electromotive forces. The measurement calibration and specimen-removed control are therefore integral to the measurement. A single amplitude reading cannot by itself distinguish microscopic alignment from a change in individual magnetic dipole moments.

Barkhausen effect
Words: 1k Articles: 3
Ferromagnetism OurBigBook.com
The Barkhausen effect consists of abrupt magnetization changes during a smooth applied magnetic field sweep. Its inductive signal is Barkhausen noise, often arising from collective magnetic domain wall motion.[ref]
The distinction is between a smooth drive and an intermittent material response. A smooth macroscopic hysteresis curve can hide smaller jumps. By Faraday's law of induction, a pickup coil responds to the rate of change of linked magnetic flux, so a rapid jump can be conspicuous even when the total change is small. A pulse is not one chemical atom flipping: neither its height nor the number of audible clicks counts individual electron spins. Qualitative crackling alone does not establish quantum spin; collective switching also admits a classical model with trapped interfaces. Compare the distinct mechanical readout of angular momentum transfer in the Einstein-de Haas effect.
Inductive Barkhausen experiment
Words: 459
Barkhausen effect OurBigBook.com
Heinrich Barkhausen's 1919 report used iron, a 300-turn pickup coil, moving magnet, amplified telephone readout and galvanometer. Removing iron corrected drive pickup. [ref]
A modern primary experiment by Gianfranco Durin and Stefano Zapperi used annealed iron–silicon strips and amorphous alloys. A 60 cm solenoid swept a triangular magnetic field intensity; a 50-turn pickup coil, wound within 1 mm, sensed the specimen. A preamplifier with a 3–20 kHz low-pass filter preceded sampling. Measurements selected the central hysteresis region dominated by magnetic domain wall motion. Above-background threshold crossings defined event durations; integrating between crossings defined event sizes. These are reported procedures, rather than data generated for the diagrams.[ref]
For this stationary implementation, secure a thin ferromagnet and its pickup coil inside a longer drive solenoid, keeping their relative positions fixed. Drive the solenoid with a slow triangular electric current, monitor that electric current, and record the amplified, filtered induced electromotive force with a digitizer. A speaker may make suitable frequencies audible, but the voltage record is needed for quantitative analysis. Slow variation of the drive does not require smooth magnetization. A triangular drive supplies an approximately constant applied-field sweep rate along each ramp; it does not guarantee constant instantaneous dM/dt.
A proposed control sequence makes the inference testable. First record the electronics background with no drive. Repeat the same sweep with the specimen removed, retaining coil geometry: mutual induction from the drive can itself induce a voltage. A matching empty pickup coil wired in opposition can suppress common drive pickup, after checking its matching. Compensation of air flux by an opposed coil is an established method.[ref] Then restore the specimen, repeat both sweep directions, reduce sweep rate, and compare the same hysteresis region with fixed amplifier gain, filter and threshold. Monitor drive irregularities and mechanical vibration; either can generate spurious pulses. These controls are recommendations for the schematic, rather than undocumented controls attributed to the modern paper.
A genuine material contribution should differ from the blank-coil record and change reproducibly with the magnetic preparation and sweep region. Quieting the drive tests drive-correlated pickup, but a held field need not eliminate all delayed material motion. Reversing the sweep is a consistency check on signed changes, not a demand that individual events retrace. A changing pulse count under a different filter or threshold cannot by itself establish changed microscopic dynamics. The useful inference is intermittent collective magnetization change within the instrument's signal bandwidth, with spatial detail left unresolved.

Write the magnetic flux linkage of the stationary pickup coil as λ=∑n=1N​Φn​, in SI units of weber. If every turn links the same magnetic flux Φ, then λ=NΦ; the turn count is dimensionless. With a fixed winding and terminal convention, Faraday's law of induction gives the induced electromotive force
e(t)=−dtdλ​,∫ta​tb​​e(t)dt=−[λ(tb​)−λ(ta​)].

This is the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to magnetic flux linkage. Its units are Vs=Wb, not volts alone. Reversing the leads reverses the sign. Separate direct drive linkage from material linkage: λ=λdrive​+λmaterial​. Even an empty pickup coil has −dλdrive​/dt. In an ideal long, uniformly coupled specimen with negligible demagnetizing field correction and eddy current shielding, a useful material approximation is

(43)

Finite geometry and nonuniform magnetization generally require a calibrated coupling in place of μ0​NAs​. The exact linkage identity survives that failure of the uniform approximation.
As an original illustrative calculation, stipulate N=100, As​=10−6m2, ΔM=103A/m and rounded μ0​=4π×10−7Vs/(Am). Then
Δλ=4π×10−8Wb≈0.125664μWb,∫ematerial​dt≈−0.125664mVms.
(44)
A uniform change over 0.10ms would give a rectangular pulse of −1.25664mV; over 0.20ms it gives −0.628319mV with the same area. Thus pulse height mixes change size with change speed. These numbers describe an ideal model, not observed pulses or material constants.

This ideal filter models resolution, rather than claiming the cited instrument had exactly this response.
The nearby positive jumps in the figure have additive negative pulse areas even when their tails overlap. The total signed area still records the sum if the complete response is integrated, but cannot identify how that sum was partitioned into events. Equal simultaneous jumps are exactly indistinguishable from a single jump of their summed size in this linear measurement. Oppositely signed simultaneous changes can cancel.
Area preservation requires the stated electronics. A zero-DC stage after the low-pass filter has response

Consequently ∫G(q∗h∗ejump​)(t)dt=0 over the complete response: a main pulse is followed by a compensating tail. Integrating only a threshold-selected lobe, clipping the record, or saturating the amplifier breaks the simple pulse-area inference. Recovering a magnetization change from such a readout needs the calibrated frequency response and an appropriate reconstruction. Neither the audible crackle nor the displayed voltage is a direct staircase of magnetization.

Magnetic dipole moment (m)

A magnetic dipole moment is a vector that summarizes the strength and orientation of a localized magnetic source. For a planar current loop, it is the electric current times the vector area: m=IAn. The right-hand rule fixes the unit normal vector n: curl the fingers of the right hand along the conventional current, and the thumb points along m. This single vector predicts both the distant magnetic dipole field and the turning effect of an imposed magnetic field.[ref]
The SI unit is ampere times square metre, Am2, equivalently joule per tesla. A magnetic dipole moment is neither a magnetic field nor a magnetic monopole: a closed current loop can have a nonzero magnetic dipole moment while its net outward magnetic flux through any closed surface remains zero, as required by Gauss's law for magnetism.
For a localized, steady electric current density J(r), the more general definition is
m=21​∫R3​r×J(r)d3r.
(64)
Here the cross product is integrated over the complete source, including return paths. Steadiness requires ∇⋅J=0, and localization requires sufficiently rapid decay for the boundary terms to vanish. Under these assumptions the localized steady-current moment identities give ∫Jd3r=0: shifting the origin by a changes the proposed magnetic dipole moment by −21​a×∫Jd3r=0. An isolated open wire segment does not satisfy these assumptions. [ref].

Barnett effect

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Magnetic dipole moment OurBigBook.com Tags: Magnetization
The Barnett effect is the change of a body's magnetization caused by mechanical rotation. Turning the whole specimen can bias the internal angular momentum carrying its magnetic moments, even with zero applied magnetic field. It is the reciprocal physical question to the Einstein-de Haas effect: impose rotation and measure magnetization, rather than change magnetization and observe mechanical motion. The relation between the two becomes especially transparent when the same signed gyromagnetic ratio connects magnetic moment and internal angular momentum.
Samuel Jackson Barnett published Magnetization by Rotation on 1 October 1915 in Physical Review. The Barnett rotation magnetometry experiment below provides an inspected modern example. The important distinction is between an equivalent term in a Hamiltonian and the actual external magnetic field measured by a magnetometer: the first biases the material; its resulting magnetization produces the second.
Barnett equivalent magnetic field (BΩ​=Ω/γ)
Words: 271
Barnett effect OurBigBook.com
Let the specimen rotate uniformly with angular velocity Ω=Ωz. In its rotating reference frame, the internal Hamiltonian contains
Hrot​=H0​−ΩJz​.
(65)
Here Jz​ is the internal angular momentum operator about the rotation axis, and H0​ contains the internal interactions and any imposed magnetic field expressed in that frame. It does not include the separately treated rigid body's rotational kinetic energy. For a sector with magnetic moment mz​=γJz​, the rotational term has exactly the form of a magnetic dipole potential energy:
−ΩJz​=−mz​BΩ​,BΩ​=γΩ​.
(66)
This Barnett equivalent magnetic field has tesla units, with the angular convention for the signed gyromagnetic ratio: Ω is in radians per second, not revolutions per second. Its sign matters. For an electronic contribution with γ<0, positive Ω favors positive Jz​ and negative mz​. A sector with γ>0 has the opposite magnetic sign. Equal Ω need not correspond to equal Barnett fields for sectors having different gyromagnetic ratios.
A short derivation fixes the sign independently of any material model. Put U(t)=exp(−iΩtJz​/ℏ) and transform a laboratory quantum state by ∣ψrot​⟩=U†∣ψlab​⟩. The Schrödinger equation gives
Hrot​=U†Hlab​U−iℏU†U˙=H0​−ΩJz​.
(67)
The transformed laboratory term is denoted by H0​; a laboratory perturbation not stationary in the rotating frame can make it time dependent. Establishing a steady thermal response also requires exchange of internal angular momentum with the rotating body, for example through spin-lattice relaxation. A mere relabeling of coordinates cannot polarize isolated, unrelaxed spins.
The Barnett field is a useful description of spin-rotation coupling, not a claim that empty laboratory space acquires a uniform magnetic flux density Ω/γ. In particular, inserting it into the Lorentz force on an unrelated test electric charge is unjustified. A nearby magnetometer detects the specimen's actual stray magnetic field and backgrounds, rather than directly detecting this internal Hamiltonian parameter.

At positive temperature T, thermal equilibrium with the rotating lattice gives energy levels E±​=∓ℏΩ/2. Define the dimensionless variable x=ℏΩ/(2kB​T), where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant and kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. The partition function and Boltzmann distribution give
Z=ex+e−x=2coshx,p+​=Zex​,p−​=Ze−x​.

⟨Jz​⟩=2ℏ​tanhx,⟨mz​⟩=γ2ℏ​tanhx,Mz​=nγ2ℏ​tanhx,

where n is number density. This is the rotational version of the independent-moment magnetic response. The angular momentum aligns with positive rotation even when the magnetic moment points oppositely. The probability ratio p+​/p−​=e2x provides a direct population check of the sign.
For ∣x∣≪1, expand the hyperbolic tangent to obtain

The slope against BΩ​ is positive for either sign of γ, while the slope against Ω has the sign of γ. At fixed T>0, reversing Ω reverses both means, and Ω=0 gives zero. At fixed nonzero Ω, the formal T→0+ limit saturates ∣⟨Jz​⟩∣ at ℏ/2; the linear approximation must not be extrapolated there. At T→∞, the response vanishes. These limits describe the toy canonical ensemble, whose equilibration is assumed.

Keeping a rotor at prescribed Ω while its internal angular momentum changes requires the drive to supply the appropriate angular impulse. In an isolated body the mechanical part instead changes oppositely, as in magnetomechanical angular momentum balance. There is no creation of net angular momentum by choosing a rotating frame.

The two-state calculation is not a general formula for a ferromagnet. Exchange interactions, magnetic domains, magnetic domain-wall pinning, magnetic anisotropy, and hysteresis can determine which response is accessible. Both spin angular momentum and orbital angular momentum can contribute; a single constant gyromagnetic ratio may be only a restricted effective description. Rotation sets an internal bias, while the material and its preparation determine magnetization. The Barkhausen effect illustrates why a smooth bias can produce jumps instead of the toy smooth curve.
For a limited, reversible, isotropic linear model, suppose the same intrinsic volume magnetic susceptibility χv​ responds to the applied bias and to BΩ​/μ0​. For a uniformly magnetized ellipsoid along a principal axis, include its demagnetizing factor Nd​:

Mz​=1+Nd​χv​χv​​(Happ​+μ0​γΩ​).

In SI, dimensionless χv​ multiplies an intensity in A/m, so Mz​=χv​Ω/γ would omit μ0​ and have the wrong units. A susceptibility defined instead as ∂M/∂B has different units. State the convention before comparing formulas.
At zero applied magnetic field intensity, a stipulated χv​=3 gives prefactor 3/2 in a sphere, with Nd​=1/3, and a prefactor approaching 3 in a long axial ellipsoid. This is a geometry check of the assumed linear model. A real cylinder does not have an exactly uniform demagnetizing field, and an irreversible ferromagnet cannot in general be represented by this single linear equation. Einstein-de Haas effect

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Magnetic dipole moment OurBigBook.com
The Einstein-de Haas effect is mechanical rotation or twisting caused by a change in a body's magnetization. The microscopic carriers of magnetic dipole moment also carry angular momentum: changing their net orientation can transfer angular momentum to the body. A freely suspended ferromagnet can therefore turn when its magnetization reverses. A suspension instead stores part of the response as an elastic twist. This makes a microscopic property accessible through a macroscopic angle.
The central measurement compares a change of magnetic dipole moment with transferred angular momentum, giving a gyromagnetic ratio. It complements an ordinary magnetic dipole torque measurement: even with the applied magnetic field parallel to the suspension axis, so that an ideal axial magnetic dipole moment has m×B=0, changing magnetization can drive an axial twist. The external drive supplies energy; conservation of angular momentum still requires accounting for the suspension and any external axial torque.
Magnetomechanical angular momentum balance (τEdH​=−m˙z​/γ)
Words: 324
Einstein-de Haas effect OurBigBook.com
Let mz​=∫V​Mz​dV be the axial magnetic dipole moment, where Mz​ is the axial magnetization. Write Jz​ for the internal angular momentum associated with that magnetic dipole moment, and Iθ˙ for the body's rotational angular momentum, with moment of inertia I. In a regime admitting a constant signed gyromagnetic ratio mz​=γJz​, axial conservation of angular momentum gives
dtd​(Iθ˙+Jz​)=τext​,Iθ¨=τext​−γm˙z​​,τEdH​=−γm˙z​​.
(75)
Here τEdH​ names the internal reaction torque on the body, not an additional external torque. The external term includes the suspension. The model assumes that the changing internal angular momentum is transferred to the measured mechanical motion, with other storage or escape channels negligible on the observation timescale. A changing or non-collinear mixture of orbital angular momentum and spin angular momentum need not admit a single constant γ.
During a reversal fast compared with the mechanical response, with negligible external angular impulse, integrating the balance gives
ΔLbody​=−ΔJz​=−γΔmz​​.
(76)
For mz​:+ms​→−ms​ and an electronic γ<0, the body acquires ΔLbody​=2ms​/γ<0: its initial rotation is toward −z by the right-hand rule. Reversing the reversal reverses the impulse. Over a complete periodic cycle, Δmz​=0, so the net reaction angular impulse vanishes; a resonant alternating response does not imply steadily accumulating angular momentum.
The orbital angular momentum prediction can be derived without a material model. A charge q traveling around a circle of radius r at angular frequency ω has loop electric current qω/(2π) and magnetic dipole moment m=qωr2/2. Its orbital angular momentum is L=me​ωr2, hence, for an electron with electric charge −e,
mL​=−2me​e​L,γL​=−2me​e​.
(77)
The electron magnetic moment associated with intrinsic spin instead obeys
mS​=−gs​2me​e​S,γS​=−gs​2me​e​,gs​≃2.
(78)
Here e>0 is the elementary charge, me​ is the electron mass, and gs​ is the electron spin g-factor.[ref] Thus the same change of magnetic dipole moment corresponds to about half as much transferred angular momentum in the pure-spin model as in the orbital angular momentum model. This factor of two is a relation between magnetic dipole moment and angular momentum, not evidence that an electron is literally a rotating charged sphere. In a material with both contributions, the inferred coefficient is a material-dependent magnetomechanical gyromagnetic ratio.
Einstein-de Haas experiment
Words: 319
Einstein-de Haas effect OurBigBook.com
In 1915, Albert Einstein and Wander Johannes de Haas suspended a soft-iron cylinder by glass fibre between coaxial coils. Alternating magnetization drove torsional resonance; a mirror reflected lamplight onto a scale. They compensated Earth's magnetic field, tilted the coils, and rotated the suspension attachment to test unwanted magnetic dipole torques. Added known moment of inertia calibrated the mechanical response.[ref]
Their paper acknowledges a failed phase determination and claims only ten-percent precision for the revised measurement. Its agreement with the orbital gyromagnetic ratio prediction was not a direct discovery of spin.[ref] Comparing that orbital gyromagnetic ratio prediction with the electron spin g-factor explains why a successful qualitative demonstration of angular momentum transfer can coexist with an inadequate quantitative interpretation. The stated precision is the authors' estimate; it does not establish that all systematic errors were bounded by that amount.
The general control problem follows directly from the model. Unwanted magnetic dipole torque can drive the same mechanical resonance as the desired reaction torque. In the ideal geometry mz​ and Bz​ alone produce no axial cross product, but transverse magnetic dipole moments, stray transverse magnetic fields and imperfect alignment can. Nulling stray magnetic fields and deliberately varying alignment test this contribution. Merely observing a large resonant twist cannot identify its cause.
For a nearly instantaneous magnetic response, a sinusoidal magnetization makes mz​ follow the drive while −m˙z​/γ is in phase quadrature. An ordinary magnetic contribution proportional to mz​ is then distinguishable by phase, after removing the mechanical frequency response. Hysteresis or delayed magnetic response can spoil this simple separation. The measured magnetization, rather than the coil electric current alone, must set the reference. Mechanical vibration, magnetostriction coupled through imperfect geometry, and changing suspension properties require separate checks; none is eliminated simply by reversing the coil electric current.

A fixed-amplitude reference torque τc​cosωt measures ∣Hτ​∣ directly. The Einstein-de Haas effect instead contains an extra factor ω when m1​ stays fixed. Consequently its twist amplitude peaks exactly at ω0​ in this model, whereas the fixed-torque peak is at ω0​1−1/(2Q2)​ when Q>1/2​. To verify the first statement, divide the squared denominator of AEdH​ by ω2: the quantity to minimize is (κ/ω−Iω)2+b2, minimized at ω0​. Both response curves tend to zero at high frequency; only the magnetomechanical curve also tends to zero at zero frequency.

An externally imposed magnetic field that is nearly uniform over a rigid current loop produces the torque

The magnetic dipole potential energy uses a dot product, whereas the torque uses a cross product. The torque is largest when the magnetic dipole moment is perpendicular to the magnetic field; parallel alignment minimizes the potential energy.[ref]

τz​=−mBsinθ=−dθdU​.

Both parallel and antiparallel alignment have zero torque, but they are respectively a stable equilibrium and an unstable equilibrium. With no damping, a freely released current loop can undergo oscillation around the stable equilibrium; settling requires damping.
In the twelve-turn example, take B=0.020T and θ=60°. The predicted torque is τz​=−2.35×10−4Nm and the magnetic dipole potential energy is U=−1.36×10−4J. The unit check is (Am2)T=Nm=J; torque and energy have the same physical dimensions but different physical meanings.
A short derivation starts with the magnetic force on a current-carrying wire, dF=Idr×Bext​. In an exactly uniform magnetic field, the net force is I(∮C​dr)×Bext​=0, but its torque need not vanish: opposite sides produce a turning couple. Integrating r×dF gives m×Bext​. Integrating dU=−τz​dθ at fixed m and B gives the orientation potential energy. This is the mechanical orientation potential energy for a maintained electric current, with the external source held fixed; the energy accounting for field and power supply is a separate problem. A varying external magnetic field requires corrections across a finite current loop, and can also give a net force.

For a quantitative repeat, independently check that conversion with known forces at a measured perpendicular lever arm, and check the imposed magnetic field at the test current loop. These are proposed calibration checks, not additional measurements reported here. The ideal Helmholtz coil model predicts
B0​=(54​)3/2RH​μ0​NH​IH​​,∣τ∣=NIπR2B0​∣sinθ∣,

where NH​ and RH​ are the winding count and radius of each field-producing Helmholtz coil, distinct from N and R of the test current loop. Derive B0​ by adding the on-axis magnetic field of a circular current loop at distances RH​/2 from both coils. Independently calibrating B0​ and the restoring torque lets a fitted torque amplitude determine m as amplitude divided by B0​, to compare with NIπR2.
Useful additional controls are to reverse only I, reverse only IH​, and reverse both: the signed torque should reverse in either single reversal and be unchanged in the double reversal. Repeat angular settings in both directions to reveal lead-dependent offsets. These are suggested controls. Limits include finite magnetic field uniformity, uncertainty in effective winding area and angular zero, meter calibration, Joule heating, and residual lead torque. An apparently sinusoidal trace alone does not establish the absolute magnetic dipole moment. No raw laboratory data or new measured values are claimed here.

Polykarp Kusch and Henry Michael Foley compared hyperfine structure resonance frequencies for different electronic states of gallium, indium and sodium. Their 1948 paper reports mutually consistent departures from the ratios expected with orbital factor 1 and spin factor 2. Comparing several states constrained the alternative explanation of perturbed atomic levels.[ref]
The Rabi molecular beam magnetic resonance experiment explains the readout principle: a resonant transition changes an atom's magnetic response, and hence its transmitted beam signal. Kusch describes rapidly interchangeable ovens, several radio frequency oscillators and careful field homogenization. Measurements taken during monotonic field drift were reduced to a common field.[ref]
Real hyperfine structure lines are not simply bare electronic gJ​ times field. Nuclear magnetic moments, known interaction constants and nonlinear field dependence enter the inference.[ref] Field homogeneity controls line broadening; alternating species addresses drift. Neither control removes an error in the atomic model. The beauty of the comparison is the separation of two problems: cancelling a shared calibration scale and testing whether several physical systems imply the same electron spin g-factor.

Words: 2k Articles: 7
Electromagnetism OurBigBook.com
For a steady current density J, the magnetic field is
B(r)=4πμ0​​∫∣r−r′∣3J(r′)×(r−r′)​d3r′.
(102)
The Biot-Savart law adds magnetic field contributions from a specified electric current distribution. The vectors r′ and r locate source and observer; r−r′ points toward the observer. Here μ0​ is vacuum permeability. For a thin wire carrying electric current I, the volume integral becomes a line integral:
B(r)=4πμ0​I​∫C​∣r−r′∣3dℓ′×(r−r′)​,dB=4πμ0​​R2Idℓ′×R​,R=r−r′.
(103)
Here dℓ′ follows positive conventional current; R is the unit vector toward the observer. With fixed path orientation, reversing the electric current replaces I by −I. The cross product and right-hand rule fix the direction. Reversing the source-to-observer displacement would give the wrong sign.[ref]
The setting is magnetostatics: time-independent current density and charge density, in vacuum or with the vacuum approximation for air. Electric charge conservation then gives ∇⋅J=0. A finite segment is part of a complete electrical circuit; its endpoints cannot continuously accumulate electric charge in a steady state. The instantaneous integral above does not describe switching transients or electromagnetic radiation. In magnetic matter, specify the total current density, including magnetization current, rather than automatically replacing μ0​ by an arbitrary magnetic permeability.[ref]
The superposition principle makes the Biot-Savart law useful even when the complete electrical circuit lacks the symmetry needed to evaluate Ampère's circuital law directly. Integrate a straight piece, a curved piece, and the return path separately, then add their magnetic fields as vectors. The beauty is that a local oriented current element produces both the circulating magnetic field of a finite straight wire and the reinforcing on-axis magnetic field of a circular current loop.
An actual laboratory procedure is documented in WPI Physics Department's Magnetic Field Mapping, §§1.2–1.2.3 and the single-coil checklist on p. 9. Preparation locates the active area of a Hall effect sensor using a small magnet. A field meter reads the component normal to that area. The wire apparatus is a wall-mounted square loop selectable between one and five conductors. The coil connects to a power supply and ammeter; its diameter and turn count are recorded. Align the sensor and scan distance. The control is a current-off background reading at each position, subtracted from the current-on reading. The inference compares corrected magnetic field with position and the predicted geometry dependence. Active-area displacement, sensor tilt, background variation, and finite coil width limit that comparison. These are instructions, not reported measurements.[ref]
A further proposed control is to reverse I at fixed sensor position and orientation. If the background and meter offset stay unchanged, the odd part isolates the magnetic field from the electric current:
2Bread​(+I)−Bread​(−I)​=Bcurrent​.
(104)
This is a deduction from the superposition principle, not a reported WPI measurement. The measured component, sensor position, and complete return path must still match the model.

Magnetic anisotropy is a directional dependence of a material's magnetic properties. A preferred direction must be distinguished from an externally imposed magnetic field.

A magnetic energy preference for an axis, with the two opposite directions equivalent in a purely uniaxial model. An easy-axis energy can be written Ksin2θ for K>0. A unidirectional term distinguishes the two directions and can instead shift a hysteresis.

Unidirectional magnetic anisotropy

Magnetic anisotropy OurBigBook.com
A directional magnetic preference that distinguishes a Magnetization direction from its reverse, unlike a purely uniaxial easy-axis energy. A pinned interface can supply such a preference and produce exchange bias. In a simple model its interfacial energy term is proportional to −Jint​cosθ.

Exchange bias (HE​)

Words: 67
Magnetic anisotropy OurBigBook.com
A displacement of a ferromagnetic hysteresis loop's field centre caused by coupling to a prepared, sufficiently pinned magnetic environment, commonly an antiferromagnet. Field cooling through the ordering/blocking range can establish a unidirectional interfacial spin preference. With switching fields H−​,H+​, the shift is HE​=(H+​+H−​)/2, distinct from coercive half-width (H+​−H−​)/2. Reversing the cooling field, testing a full major loop and comparing uncoupled/zero-field-cooled controls help identify genuine bias.

Oscillatory spacer-mediated exchange (Eex​/A=−J(t)m^1​⋅m^2​)

Words: 69
Interlayer exchange coupling OurBigBook.com
Electrons reflected by two magnetic interfaces can mediate an interaction across a nonmagnetic metal spacer. The phase accumulated on traversing the spacer varies with its thickness, producing oscillatory contributions to J(t) from Fermi surface spanning vectors. In the sign convention in the title, positive J favours parallel moments and negative J antiparallel moments. Multiple periods, interface phase shifts, disorder and finite temperature prevent a universal sign rule based on thickness alone.

Magnetism OurBigBook.com
Diamagnetism is a magnetic response in which the induced magnetization opposes the applied magnetic field intensity. In a linear isotropic description, M=χH with negative magnetic susceptibility χ.

Diamagnetic levitation in an inverse-height field (z03​=−χ(B0​r0​)2/(μ0​ρg))

Words: 58
Diamagnetism OurBigBook.com
A small weakly susceptible sphere has induced magnetic energy −χVB2/(2μ0​) and vertical force χVBB′/μ0​. In field magnitude B=B0​r0​/z, balancing gravity gives the title height for χ<0. The vertical force varies as z−3, giving a restoring derivative at that equilibrium. Three-dimensional trapping cannot be established from an axial field magnitude alone; lateral field geometry and Maxwell constraints also matter.

Landau diamagnetism

Words: 59
Diamagnetism OurBigBook.com
Landau diamagnetism is the orbital response of mobile electrons to an applied magnetic field, arising from quantization of their transverse motion. For a noninteracting three-dimensional isotropic electron gas with quadratic dispersion, electron spin with g=2 and magnetic fields weak enough for the smooth-response limit, its susceptibility is χL​=−χP​/3, where χP​ is the Pauli paramagnetism susceptibility. Band effective masses, interactions, dimensionality and resolved magnetic quantum oscillations can change this simple relation.

Magnetic order

Words: 982 Articles: 5
Magnetism OurBigBook.com
Magnetic order is a reproducible spatial organization of microscopic magnetic moments. A net magnetization describes their sum; a staggered magnetization describes an alternating pattern. These are different order parameters. For example, an alternating row of equal up and down arrows has zero sum but a definite pattern, whereas randomly oriented arrows can have a small sum without that pattern.

Short-range order
